Newton's Method with a Modified Hessian

Source: R/second_order.R
newton.Rd

Solves \(H d = -g\) for the direction, repairing \(H\) when it is not positive definite, and then performs a line search along it. The method converges quadratically near a minimum.

Usage

newton(
  criterion = crit_any(crit_grad(), crit_abs_obj(), crit_abs_par()),
  modify = modify_eigen(),
  step = 1,
  line_search = armijo(),
  maxit = 200,
  max_eval = Inf,
  verbose = FALSE,
  refresh = 10,
  keep_trace = FALSE,
  max_length = Inf,
  typical_size = NULL,
  stop_decrement = 0.001
)

Arguments

criterion

The stopping rule, a criterion() object. Defaults to crit_any(crit_grad(), crit_abs_obj(), crit_abs_par()); see crit_any() for the effect of that disjunction.

modify

A hessian_modification() object that determines how an indefinite or nearly singular Hessian is repaired before the step. A character string is rejected. The constructors are:

  • modify_eigen() (default): raises the eigenvalues of the Hessian that are below a floor to the floor.

  • modify_ridge(): adds a multiple of the identity, doubled until the Cholesky factorization succeeds.

  • A user-defined subclass of hessian_modification() with a method for hessian_modify(), which needs no change to this function.

The floor is an argument of the constructor, as in newton(modify = modify_ridge(floor = 1e-6)). See modifications for the comparison and hessian_modify() for writing a new object.

step

Initial step length offered to the line search, a single positive number. Defaults to 1, which is the Newton step itself and is accepted unchanged near the solution.

line_search

A line_search() object. Defaults to armijo(). The curvature condition that bfgs() needs is unnecessary here, because the curvature is read from the Hessian.

maxit, max_eval, verbose, refresh, keep_trace

As in optimizer(). maxit defaults to 200 here and to 500 in bfgs() and lbfgs(): a Newton run that has not converged in 200 iterations usually has a problem that more iterations do not solve.

max_length

The largest component that a step may have, a single positive number. A direction longer than this in the infinity norm is scaled down to this length before the line search. Defaults to Inf, which leaves every step as it is. See below.

typical_size

NULL (the default), or the typical size of each parameter: one positive number, or one per parameter. Every length used by the method is then measured in these units, as the largest \(\lvert d_i\rvert / t_i\) in place of the largest \(\lvert d_i\rvert\): the bound max_length, and the scaling of a direction whose length is not set by the curvature. With NULL the lengths are measured in the units of the parameters.

stop_decrement

The largest Newton decrement \(\tfrac12 g^\top H^{-1} g\) at which a stopping rule on the change in the parameters or in the objective, such as crit_abs_par() or crit_abs_obj(), may end the run as converged. A single positive number, in the units of the objective, or Inf to accept every such stop. Defaults to 1e-3. See below.

Value

An S7 object of class Newton, inheriting from optimizer(), to be handed to minimize().

Why the Hessian has to be repaired

\(-H^{-1}g\) is guaranteed to be a descent direction only when \(H\) is positive definite. Where the objective curves downwards the unmodified step can point towards a saddle or a maximum, and a line search along an ascent direction cannot decrease the objective. Indefinite Hessians are common far from the solution.

The repair is selected by modify. Every repair begins with an attempted Cholesky factorization, which, when it succeeds, is both the test for positive definiteness and the solve. When it fails, the Hessian is passed to hessian_modify() and the two shipped repairs are:

modify_eigen()

decompose \(H\) and raise every eigenvalue below \(\max(\texttt{floor}, \texttt{floor}\,\max_i\lvert\lambda_i\rvert)\) to that value. The direction is then the Newton direction in the subspace where the curvature is positive, and close to the gradient direction in the rest. The repair costs a symmetric eigendecomposition and gives the best-conditioned matrix. If the eigendecomposition fails, the ridge repair is used.

modify_ridge()

add \(\tau I\) and double \(\tau\) until the factorization succeeds. This is Levenberg's idea: it interpolates between the Newton step at \(\tau = 0\) and a scaled steepest-descent step for large \(\tau\). It costs less than the eigendecomposition and shifts every eigenvalue, not only the small ones.

A user-defined hessian_modification() is called through R at each such iterate. A repair of the Hessian is recorded in the trace as hessian modified, or hessian modified (capped) when the repaired step is also scaled down (see below). The label does not record which repair was used.

Bounding the length of a step

The Newton step minimizes the local quadratic model of the objective, and its length is set by the curvature at the current point. Where the objective flattens towards an asymptote the curvature is small and the step is long, and it can carry the iterate past the minimum into the flat region. The line search accepts such a step whenever it lowers the objective, and in the flat region the gradient is close to zero, so the run can stop there. Such steps occur, for example, when a smoothing parameter is optimized on the logarithmic scale.

max_length bounds the step; it is the maxstep of the line-search Newton method of Dennis and Schnabel (1983) and the maxNstep of the smoothing-parameter iteration of mgcv. The bound only shortens a step, and near a minimum the Newton steps are short, so the quadratic convergence of the method is kept. A step shortened by the bound is recorded in the trace as newton step capped, except at an iteration at which the Hessian was repaired, which keeps the label of the repair.

Stopping on the change

A rule on the change in the parameters or in the objective ends the run when the iterate stops moving, which near a minimum is the same as having arrived. Away from a minimum it is not. Where the Hessian has no Cholesky factor, the step that preceded the stop came from the repaired matrix and its length is the floor's, so that a Hessian with a very large eigenvalue and a negative one yields steps of the order of \(10^{-8}\) while the objective is still falling. Where the Hessian is positive definite, a step that is short for another reason, such as a bound max_length, leaves the Newton decrement \(\tfrac12 g^\top H^{-1} g\), the decrease that the quadratic model still predicts, above what a minimum would leave.

A stop on the change is therefore not accepted at a point where the Hessian is not positive definite or where the Newton decrement exceeds stop_decrement. The run ends as not converged, with criterion_met reporting "stopped without converging" and the message giving the reason, and the trace records the safeguard change stop refused. A rule on the gradient, such as crit_grad(), is not affected, and neither is a point at which the Hessian is not finite. The check costs one Hessian evaluation at the point where such a stop would end the run. stop_decrement = Inf accepts every stop on a change, as in versions before 0.17.0.

Parameters in different units

A length in the units of the parameters has different meanings for parameters on different scales: a displacement of one is a long step for a parameter on the log scale and a short one for a variance of several hundred. typical_size gives the typical size \(t_i\) of each parameter, as in the scaled norm of Dennis and Schnabel (1983): every length is then the largest \(\lvert d_i\rvert / t_i\), for the bound max_length and for the scaling of a repaired direction or of a gradient fallback.

The length of a repaired step

Where the factorization succeeds, \(-H^{-1}g\) is the Newton step and step = 1 is its natural unit, so the step is taken as it stands, subject only to max_length. Where it fails, the component of the direction in the floored subspace is \(g_i/\lambda_{\mathrm{floor}}\), whose size is set by the floor of the modification and not by the curvature of the objective. The direction is therefore multiplied by \(\min(1, 1/\lVert d\rVert_\infty)\), which gives a displacement of order one in the parameters. bfgs() and lbfgs() apply the same rule to their first direction. The factor never exceeds one, so a run whose repaired steps were already of order one is unchanged. The same scaling applies to the gradient direction that the method uses when a solve fails.

Without this factor the length of a repaired step is bounded only by the line search, at one objective evaluation per backtrack. Each backtrack can be expensive, for example a complete penalized refit when the objective is a marginal criterion.

The Hessian by differences

When hess is not supplied to minimize() the Hessian is obtained by differencing the gradient. With an analytic gradient that is one numerical differentiation. When the gradient is also differenced, the Hessian is a difference of differences, which happens only in newton() and chebyshev(): one Newton iteration then costs about \(4p^2\) evaluations of the objective, against about \(2p\) evaluations of the gradient with an analytic gradient. For an objective without either derivative, bfgs(), which needs no Hessian, is usually cheaper.

References

Dennis, J. E. and Schnabel, R. B. (1983). Numerical Methods for Unconstrained Optimization and Nonlinear Equations. Prentice-Hall, Englewood Cliffs, NJ.

Gill, P. E., Murray, W. and Wright, M. H. (1981). Practical Optimization. Academic Press, London.

Nocedal, J. and Wright, S. J. (2006). Numerical Optimization, 2nd edition. Springer, New York.

See also

modifications for the repairs of the Hessian, modify_eigen(), modify_ridge() and hessian_modify() to write another, bfgs() and lbfgs() when a Hessian is not available, armijo() for the line search, summary.optimizer_result() for the safeguard counts.

Examples

rosen <- function(p) (1 - p[1])^2 + 100 * (p[2] - p[1]^2)^2
rosen_gr <- function(p) c(-2 * (1 - p[1]) - 400 * p[1] * (p[2] - p[1]^2),
                          200 * (p[2] - p[1]^2))
rosen_he <- function(p) matrix(
  c(2 - 400 * (p[2] - 3 * p[1]^2), -400 * p[1],
    -400 * p[1], 200), 2, 2)

minimize(newton(), rosen, c(-1.2, 1), gr = rosen_gr, hess = rosen_he)
#> <optimizer_result> Newton
#>   value      : 3.74398e-21
#>   par        : 1 1
#>   iterations : 21   evaluations: f 29, g 22
#>   elapsed    : 1 ms
#>   converged  : yes (gradient (max-norm) < 1e-06 or |df| < 1e-10 or |dx| < 1e-08)

# The repair of an indefinite Hessian is an object, with its floor.
newton(modify = modify_ridge(floor = 1e-6))
#> <optimizer> Newton
#>   stop when : gradient (max-norm) < 1e-06 or |df| < 1e-10 or |dx| < 1e-08
#>   budgets   : maxit 200, evaluations Inf
#>   settings  : step = 1, line_search = Armijo backtracking (c1 = 1e-04), modify = ridge (floor = 1e-06), max_length = Inf, typical_size = <NULL>, stop_decrement = 0.001

# At a saddle the unrepaired step points the wrong way. The Hessian at
# the start has eigenvalues 2 and -1.99; the repair is recorded in the
# trace.
sad <- function(p) p[1]^2 - p[2]^2 + 0.1 * p[2]^4
sg  <- function(p) c(2 * p[1], -2 * p[2] + 0.4 * p[2]^3)
sh  <- function(p) matrix(c(2, 0, 0, -2 + 1.2 * p[2]^2), 2, 2)
eigen(sh(c(0.5, 0.1)), only.values = TRUE)$values
#> [1]  2.000 -1.988

r <- minimize(newton(keep_trace = TRUE), sad, c(0.5, 0.1), gr = sg, hess = sh)
c(value = r@value, iterations = r@iterations)
#>      value iterations 
#>       -2.5        5.0 
unique(r@trace$safeguard)
#> [1] "hessian modified (capped)" "none"                     

# summary() counts the safeguards that fired during the run.
summary(minimize(newton(keep_trace = TRUE), rosen, c(-1.2, 1),
                 gr = rosen_gr, hess = rosen_he))
#> <optimizer_result> Newton
#>   value      : 3.74398e-21
#>   par        : 1 1
#>   iterations : 21   evaluations: f 29, g 22
#>   elapsed    : 3 ms
#>   converged  : yes (gradient (max-norm) < 1e-06 or |df| < 1e-10 or |dx| < 1e-08)
#>   safeguards :
#>     step shortened: 4
